query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, deformation at intermediate temperatures induces dynamic nanoclustering of principal elements (Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries, which lowers boundary cohesion and triggers brittle intergranular fracture, whereas at cryogenic temperatures the suppression of diffusion preserves ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA with homogeneous elemental distribution and no preexisting grain-boundary precipitates.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled tensile and creep tests at cryogenic, room, and intermediate elevated temperatures (e.g., 300–500 °C) under defined strain-rate protocols. Incorporate time-resolved in situ grain boundary characterization (using atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM) to capture the evolution of nanoclusters during deformation.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted over a range of temperatures and strain rates that maintain the alloy as a single-phase solid solution, ensuring an experimental baseline at cryogenic conditions (with suppressed diffusion) and experimental conditions at intermediate temperatures where atomic mobility begins to allow dynamic clustering.
generation.structural_mediator: Deformation-induced nanoclusters of principal elements (Cr, Ni, and Mn) forming at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under mechanical loading at intermediate temperatures, thermally activated diffusion and stress combine to cause a transient accumulation of Cr, Ni, and Mn into nanoscale clusters along the grain boundaries. This clustering compromises grain-boundary cohesion before any conventional phase precipitation or impurity segregation occurs, leading to premature intergranular fracture and a reduction in alloy toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the cryogenic baseline—where nanoclustering is suppressed and ductility is maintained—intermediate temperature tests will show the formation of nanoclusters at grain boundaries that correlate with lowered toughness and prevalent intergranular brittle fracture. Time-resolved data should reveal the onset and growth of these clusters during deformation.
generation.baseline: Performance at cryogenic temperatures, where limited diffusional mobility suppresses nanocluster formation, resulting in ductile behavior and high toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate in single-phase HEAs under service conditions that allow limited diffusion (i.e., intermediate temperatures before conventional phase separation occurs). Extreme temperatures that trigger full phase separation or where kinetic effects are negligible (such as very high cooling rate or extremely low temperatures) fall outside the scope.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence and theory support dynamic nanocluster formation, the exact temperature and strain-rate thresholds demarcating the onset of appreciable nanoclustering versus other phenomena remain uncertain. Experimental resolution and time-resolved measurement challenges may also complicate the clear isolation of this mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of tensile and creep tests on the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi HEA at carefully selected temperatures (cryogenic and intermediate, e.g., 300–500 °C) and strain rates. Utilize time-resolved in situ atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM to monitor grain boundary chemical evolution during deformation. Compare mechanical fracture modes and toughness measures between conditions.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of nanoscale clustering at grain boundaries (cluster size, density, composition) via APT/TEM during and after deformation.
Mechanical properties including fracture toughness, ductility, and fracture mode (intergranular vs. transgranular) from tensile/creep tests.
Temperature and strain-rate profiles to correlate with onset of nanocluster formation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under intermediate temperature deformation conditions, time-resolved measurements show no significant formation of nanoclusters at grain boundaries and the mechanical failure mode remains ductile (similar to the cryogenic baseline), then the hypothesis that deformation-induced nanoclustering causes brittleness in HEAs would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Recently, a new alloy design concept based on entropic contributions to the thermodynamic landscape, rather than cohesive energy, was proposed, which was subsequently extended to non-metallic systems such as multicomponent oxides. This strategy was explored by deliberately incorporating five or more elemental species into a single lattice with random site occupancy. Due to the engineered configuration disorder, these entropy-stabilized solid solution alloys, that is, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), usually show a single-phase structure with high symmetry and extremely attractive properties. Among various reported HEAs in literature, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy (also termed as Cantor's alloy) is a prototype fcc (face-centred-cubic) HEA, which possesses ultrahigh fracture toughness and large ductility, even at cryogenic temperatures. It is generally believed that HEA lattices are severely distorted and atomic diffusion is extremely sluggish due to the chemical complexity and packing disorder. Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

S4 show that the C and B composition at Cr-enriched and Ni(Mn)-enriched GBs is very low, which is insufficient to form carbides or borides at GBs. A recent study of the single-phase fcc CoFeNi2V0.5Mo0.2 HEA demonstrated that the lack of Cr and Mn can evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (). Therefore, we believe that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs can embrittle GBs and, hence, lead to ductility loss with increasing deformation temperature. Note that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs also occurs at relatively low temperatures (<700°C), which accounts for ductility loss at intermediate temperatures. In the current work, the sample after tensile test at 700°C, exhibiting remarkable ductility loss though maintaining a strain hardening capacity, provides a good model example to demonstrate our hypothesis: Nanoclustering induced GB embrittlement in HEAs at intermediate temperatures. proposals.intervention: Perform controlled tensile and creep tests at multiple temperatures and strain rates combined with in situ grain boundary characterization (e.g., atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM) to monitor elemental distributions during deformation
proposals.conditions: Tests at cryogenic, room, and intermediate elevated temperatures (e.g., 300–500 °C) under well-defined strain-rate protocols, ensuring that the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution
proposals.structural_mediator: Deformation-induced nanoclustering of principal elements (notably Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Under service conditions where diffusion is activated (but before conventional coarsening occurs), local stress and thermal activation drive subtle, dynamic segregation of the constituent elements into nanoclusters at the grain boundaries. This localized composition modulation reduces cohesive strength along the boundaries, promoting intergranular cracking under mechanical loading. In contrast to conventional alloys, where impurities or precipitates cause embrittlement, here the intrinsic multicomponent chemistry and sluggish diffusion still allow dynamic clustering that compromises boundary toughness
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline tested at cryogenic conditions (where diffusion and clustering are suppressed, preserving ductility), samples deformed at intermediate elevated temperatures will exhibit pronounced brittle intergranular fracture and lower toughness, coinciding with detection of nanoclusters at grain boundaries. Moreover, the onset of brittle behavior will correlate with the temperature/strain-rate window that permits sufficient atomic mobility but not complete phase separation.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This hypothesis directly targets the open question by pinpointing a mechanism—deformation-assisted, dynamic grain boundary nanoclustering of the principal elements—that can lead to brittle behavior even in a nominally single-phase, compositionally complex alloy. The proposed controlled comparison (varying temperature to modulate diffusional kinetics) distinguishes this mechanism from the conventional alloy behavior governed by preexisting impurity segregation and coarse brittle precipitates.

critiques.addresses_problem: The hypothesis clearly targets the open question by proposing that even in a single-phase HEA, toughness degradation can result from deformation-induced nanoclustering of the principal elements at grain boundaries—not from conventional impurity segregation or precipitate formation. This directly confronts the underlying mechanism governing brittleness in compositionally complex alloys.
critiques.constraints: It respects the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex, single-phase CrMnFeCoNi HEA and tests under defined temperature and strain-rate regimes that avoid triggering conventional phase precipitation.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound as it invokes stress- and thermally-assisted mobility within the alloy, where dynamic clustering of Cr, Ni, and Mn at grain boundaries could reduce cohesive strength. This is consistent with the evidence of nanoclustering-induced embrittlement observed in HEAs.
critiques.feasibility: The proposed experimental approach is feasible using established tensile and creep testing protocols coupled with in situ atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM for real-time characterization of grain boundary chemistry.
critiques.evidence: The direction is strongly supported by previous observations of nanocluster formation and its correlation with reduced ductility in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA, as seen in records PMC6897545 (abstract, nanoclustering induced GB embrittlement) and related evidence showing dynamic segregation at the grain boundaries.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that the dynamic nanoclustering mechanism might be confounded with other conventional segregation or grain-boundary precipitation phenomena if the temperature/strain conditions are not precisely controlled; it may be challenging to isolate the effect of dynamic clustering from preexisting microstructural heterogeneities.
critiques.fix: Implement additional time-resolved measurements to track the evolution of the nanoclusters during deformation, and refine the temperature and strain-rate windows to more clearly separate dynamic clustering from any onset of conventional segregation or phase formation.

decision.rationale: We choose Direction A because it directly targets the open question of how brittleness emerges in an initially single‐phase HEA by proposing a deformation-activated, dynamic nanoclustering mechanism at grain boundaries. The critic’s review agrees the mechanism is physically sound and feasible with the available experimental tools. The primary risk—that conventional segregation or precipitation might confound the detection of transient nanoclusters—can be mitigated by adding time-resolved measurements and refining the temperature/strain-rate windows. This fix makes the hypothesis robust and directly testable.
